e.t: This Greek LXX verb means “cheer; make good.” It describes an action that brings about good or makes a situation better, and it can also express giving encouragement or gladness. The word occurs 22 times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, so it is used more broadly than a single isolated passage. Its precise force in any verse depends on what is being made good or whom the action affects. It appears in Judges, Ruth, Psalms, and other books, showing its use across narrative and reflective settings.

ἀκλεής means “without fame” or “inglorious”: it describes someone or something lacking renown or a celebrated reputation. As an adjective, it characterizes a person, deed, or condition rather than naming an action. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs once, so its broader range cannot be established from repeated examples in that corpus. Its precise force in 3 Maccabees 4:12 depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

This adjective describes someone or something as true and truthful—reliable, genuine, and corresponding to what is right. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings, it is used 37 times, often to identify what can be trusted rather than what is false or deceptive. Its basic sense can describe a person, statement, promise, or matter that is dependable and real. The word appears across books including Exodus, Deuteronomy, Samuel, Chronicles, Job, Isaiah, and Daniel.

Alphaal, also rendered Alfaal, is a proper name used for a person in the Greek Old Testament. It is not presented here as a common word describing an action, quality, or object, so its meaning is primarily its function as a personal name. The name occurs twice in the Greek text of 1 Chronicles, in 1 Chronicles 8:11 and 8:12. Without the surrounding verse text, Scripture does not provide enough information here to explain the person’s identity or any further significance attached to the name.

e.h: A Greek LXX Word for Fox
e.t: This noun means “fox,” referring to the animal. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs eight times across eight verses, including passages in Judges, 1 Kings, Nehemiah, Psalms, Lamentations, and Song of Songs. The word can refer to one fox or more than one, depending on the sentence. Its basic meaning remains the same wherever it appears; any figurative or contextual force must come from the surrounding verse and passage.

This word is a proper name, referring to a person named “Amēachi” or “Amiakhi.” It is not presented as a general description, action, or quality, but as an identifying personal name in the Greek Old Testament (LXX). It occurs once in this corpus, in 1 Chronicles 4:16. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the name’s specific role in that passage cannot be explained further; its basic meaning is its use as a personal designation.

This verb means to open the mouth or gape wide. It describes the physical act of opening the mouth broadly, rather than expressing a particular emotion or belief. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 6:18. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the wide opening of the mouth.

This word expresses the idea “with flowers.” It is a noun in the Greek Old Testament translation, naming something associated with flowers. It occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at Ecclesiastes 12:6. Since the verse text and surrounding context are not available here, the precise object or reference in that passage cannot be explained further. Its ordinary lexical meaning remains “with flowers,” without requiring additional meanings or translation alternatives.

This noun means “setting out” or “departure”—the act of leaving one place and beginning a journey. It names a movement away from a location rather than the destination itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Numbers 33:2, so its normal meaning is clear even though the wider range of its use cannot be observed from repeated passages. The surrounding verse would be needed to explain the particular force of the word there.

This noun refers to a “settlement of a colony”—a community established away from its original homeland. It names the settlement itself, not a person or a ruler. In the LXX corpus, it occurs six times across Jeremiah and Baruch. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central meaning remains the establishment or settlement of a colony.

gl: that which is torn off; piece
d: that which is torn off; piece

e.t: This noun means “that which is torn off; piece”—something separated or removed from a larger whole. It describes a detached portion rather than the complete thing from which it came. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, once in Jeremiah and once in Lamentations. Its precise sense in either passage is shaped by the surrounding wording, but its central idea remains a piece that has been torn away or separated. This word belongs to the Greek LXX corpus, not to the Greek New Testament.

This Greek LXX verb means “recover from” or “cure.” It describes the restoration of a person from an illness or other disabling condition, focusing on becoming well again. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs four times, all in 2 Kings 5, where the word is used in statements about recovery from disease. Its basic sense is therefore practical and restorative: someone who is afflicted becomes healthy or is healed. The exact force in any one sentence depends on the surrounding passage.

This noun refers to the chief, or commanding officer, of a bodyguard. It identifies a person who leads or oversees those responsible for guarding a ruler or important officials. In the Greek Old Testament, the word occurs twice, once in 1 Samuel and once in Esther. Its precise role in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains a high-ranking leader among the bodyguard.

Asoron is a proper name, referring to a specific person or place rather than expressing a general idea or action. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Joshua 15:3. The available wording identifies it simply as “Asōrōn; Asoron,” so the name itself is the supported meaning. Its precise referent and significance depend on the surrounding passage, which is not included here.

Attalos is a proper name referring to a person named Attalos. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 1 Maccabees 15:22. Because a name identifies someone rather than describing an action or quality, its basic meaning is the person’s name itself. The surrounding verse would be needed to explain Attalos’s role or significance in that passage.

Aphphaim, also rendered Affem, is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies a named individual or designation rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The name occurs twice in the Greek text of 1 Chronicles, at 1 Chronicles 2:30 and 2:31. Because the verse text and surrounding context are not included here, its precise referent cannot be stated more narrowly. Its meaning is therefore the name itself: “Aphphaim; Affem.”

Baithar, also rendered Vethar, is a proper name identifying a particular named entity in the Greek Septuagint. It is not a general word describing an action, quality, or object, so its meaning is chiefly the name itself rather than a broader concept. This name occurs once in the Septuagint, at 2 Samuel 15:24. The available lexical form preserves the name as Baithar or Vethar, while the reference identifies its single occurrence in the Old Testament Greek corpus.

Balaam is a proper name referring to the person called Balaam, also rendered Valaam. It is not a general word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, the name occurs 61 times across 56 verses, with most occurrences in Numbers. Its first recorded occurrence is Numbers 22:5, and its final occurrence is Micah 6:5. The surrounding passage is needed to explain what Balaam is doing or what is said about him in any particular verse.

This word is a personal name, rendered “Barek” or “Varek.” It identifies an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Joshua 19:8. Because it functions as a proper name and no surrounding verse text is provided here, its significance is limited to identifying the person named in that passage; the name itself does not supply an additional definition beyond “Barek” or “Varek.”

This verb means “bud”: to begin growing or emerge as a new shoot from a plant. It describes the act of budding rather than the plant or shoot itself. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, in Ecclesiastes 2:6. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but the basic picture is plant life beginning to grow and develop. This is a concrete word that can express the early emergence of vegetation.

Bouzi, also rendered Vuzi, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a person named in Ezekiel 1:3 and occurs once in the Greek Old Testament corpus. Because the available information gives the name but no further lexical definition or surrounding verse text, its meaning is best understood as the personal name itself. The reference establishes where this name appears, while the name’s precise significance depends on the identity and context provided in that passage.

This word is a proper name, rendered “Gaibal” or “Yeval.” It identifies a named entity rather than describing an action, quality, or relationship. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs five times, appearing in Deuteronomy and Joshua. Its references are Deuteronomy 11:29, Deuteronomy 27:4, Deuteronomy 27:13, and Joshua 9:2. The surrounding verse text is needed to determine exactly whom or what the name identifies in each passage.

This noun means “creator,” referring to one who brings something into being. It presents the person or power responsible for making or originating something, rather than describing the thing that was made. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in Wisdom 13:3. The word’s precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and its wider argument, but its central meaning remains one who creates or brings forth.

Goni is a personal name, not a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies an individual in the Greek Old Testament. This name appears once in the LXX corpus, at 1 Chronicles 7:13. Because the available information gives the name and its reference but not the surrounding verse text, its lexical meaning is simply the proper name Goni; the passage itself supplies the person’s family and historical setting.

This Greek LXX verb means to “enjoin; distinctly command”—to give an instruction in a clear, definite way. It describes speech that lays out what someone is required to do, rather than a casual suggestion. The word appears 54 times in the Greek LXX, across the Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, so it can describe repeated kinds of authoritative instruction. Its exact force in any verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This noun means “teaching” or “instruction”: the giving or communicating of knowledge, guidance, or understanding. It can refer to what is taught as well as the activity of teaching. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs four times—twice in Old Testament books and twice in Sirach. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding words, but its central idea remains the communication of instruction intended to shape understanding and conduct.

This word means “two,” referring to a quantity of two people, objects, animals, or things. It functions as a number, identifying a pair or count of two rather than describing a quality or action. In the Greek Old Testament and related LXX books, it occurs 585 times, showing regular use in descriptions, lists, measurements, offerings, and other matters involving pairs or quantities. Its basic meaning remains consistent wherever it appears; the surrounding sentence determines what two things are being counted.

Eblazer, also rendered Evlazer, is a proper name identifying a person. In the Greek LXX, this name occurs once, at 2 Kings 17:31. The name itself identifies the individual but does not, by itself, state the person’s character, actions, role, or significance. Those details belong to the surrounding passage rather than to the name’s basic meaning. Thus, Eblazer is best understood simply as the personal name Eblazer or Evlazer in this Old Testament Greek corpus.

This verb means “arrange in”: it describes placing or fitting something into an ordered setting. Its basic idea is purposeful arrangement rather than merely putting something nearby. The word appears once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 4 Maccabees 6:2. Because the surrounding verse text is not available here, the particular object being arranged cannot be stated safely; however, the word itself points to the act of arranging something within an intended order or place.

This word refers to someone or something regarded as choice or elect. It functions as a noun, naming what is specially selected rather than describing an action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Numbers 11:28. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning centers on selection and special distinction. The word belongs to the Greek LXX wording and should be understood within that translation’s Old Testament setting.

This verb means “lose heart”: to become discouraged or lose inner courage. It describes a weakening of resolve rather than a physical action, and it can identify someone who no longer presses forward with confidence. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs twice, once in Psalms and once in Zechariah. The surrounding verse determines what caused the discouragement and how it is expressed there.

This Greek Old Testament verb means “try out” or “put on trial.” It describes testing someone or something to discover what it is like, whether it is genuine, or how it will respond. The word appears five times in the Greek Old Testament, with four occurrences in Deuteronomy and one in Psalms. Its basic sense is active and purposeful: a person conducts a test rather than merely encountering difficulty. The precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This word means “deer,” referring to a graceful, hoofed wild animal. It is a noun when naming the animal and can also function adjectivally when describing something associated with a deer. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 20 times across 20 verses, including passages in Deuteronomy, Psalms, Song of Songs, Kings, and Isaiah. Its normal meaning remains the animal itself; the exact force of any figurative or poetic use must be determined from the surrounding verse and passage.

Elisa is a proper name, referring to a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Septuagint, it appears four times, all in genealogical lists in Genesis and 1 Chronicles. The name is rendered “Elisa,” and the available information supports this as its complete ordinary meaning. Its significance in any particular genealogy depends on the surrounding names and passage.

Eliphalia, also rendered Elifalia, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies an individual in the Greek Old Testament tradition. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at 1 Chronicles 15:18. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the person’s specific role or significance in that passage cannot be explained from the name alone.

Elmōdad is a proper name, also represented as “Elmothath.” It identifies a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, at Genesis 10:26. The available form gives the person’s name but does not provide a separate ordinary-word definition. Its significance in that verse must therefore be understood from the surrounding passage rather than from the name alone.

This verb means “increase” or “magnify”: it describes something becoming greater, larger, or more prominent. In biblical Greek translation of the Old Testament, it can express growth in size, number, status, or recognized greatness, depending on the sentence. The word occurs 15 times across 15 Old Testament verses, from Genesis through Malachi. Its use includes descriptions involving people, blessings, and greatness, but the precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding words and subject.

This verb means “cheer in,” expressing gladness or joyful participation in something. It describes taking delight within a setting, activity, or shared experience rather than merely observing it. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, in Proverbs 8:31. The surrounding verse is needed to explain exactly how this joyful participation functions there, but the word itself points to active rejoicing or finding happiness in what is being described.

Intercession means speaking or appealing on behalf of another person. It is a noun naming this act of representing someone before a person who can respond or decide. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, this word occurs once, at 2 Maccabees 4:8. The word’s basic sense is therefore an appeal made for someone else, rather than a general request made only for oneself.

This word means “authority” or “influence”—the power or right to direct, affect, or hold sway. As a noun, it can describe authority belonging to a person or ruling power, or influence exercised over others. In the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, it occurs 61 times, showing that it is used across a broad range of passages concerning human and governing power. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding context.

This word means “from above” or “above,” describing something located higher or coming downward from a higher place. It can function as an adverb, indicating position or direction, and as a preposition, relating one thing to another in terms of height. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 33 times across 32 verses, including descriptions of things positioned above and movement or action associated with what is above. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence.

This verb means “fall asleep over,” describing the act of falling asleep while positioned over or upon something or someone. It is a verb, so it expresses an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, in two different verses. Its exact force in either passage depends on what the surrounding sentence identifies as the object or setting of the action.

This Greek LXX verb means “sprinkle upon”: to scatter or cause a liquid or other substance to fall lightly over something. It describes an action performed on a surface, object, or person rather than merely referring to sprinkling in general. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at 2 Maccabees 1:21. The precise force of the action in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the act of sprinkling something upon another thing.

This noun means “gathering together”: the act or result of people or things being brought together in one place or group. It describes a collective coming together rather than an individual action. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 2:7. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic sense remains a gathering or assembling together.

This verb means “eject” or “blurt out”: it describes forcing something out or suddenly speaking something forth. As a verb, it focuses on the act of expelling or uttering rather than on the thing produced. In this LXX corpus, it occurs six times, so its range is shown across several passages while remaining fairly uncommon. Its precise force in any verse depends on what is being expelled or spoken.

This noun means “fair weather,” referring to calm, favorable weather rather than stormy or threatening conditions. It is a simple description of weather conditions, not a title, action, or personal quality. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in Sirach 3:15. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain how this weather reference functions in that particular sentence; the word itself plainly denotes settled, pleasant weather. [Evidence: p03:word:lxx:L705564:identity; p03:word:lxx:L705564:occurrences; p01:word:lxx:L705564:reference:0]

This Greek LXX adverb means “with a good aim,” describing how an action is carried out when it is directed accurately or successfully. It functions by modifying an action rather than naming a person, object, or event. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament corpus, once in 1 Kings 22:34 and once in 2 Chronicles 18:33. Without the surrounding verse text, its precise force in each passage cannot be expanded beyond this basic sense of acting or directing something with a good aim.

Ephaath, also rendered Efaath, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a person or place in the Greek Old Testament tradition, but the available information does not establish which kind of named entity it designates. It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at Numbers 13:21. Its precise significance must therefore be determined from that passage’s surrounding text rather than from the name itself.

e.h: A Place Known as a Haunt
e.t: “Haunt” refers to a place or setting associated with someone’s repeated presence or activity. Here it functions as a noun, naming such a familiar place rather than describing an action. This LXX word appears six times, in six verses, within the deuterocanonical books of Sirach and 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding sentence and context.

This word is the proper name “Hēraklēs,” also given as “Iraklis,” referring to a person named Herakles. As a proper noun, it functions as a personal name rather than a general description, action, or quality. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs twice, in 2 Maccabees 4:19 and 4:20. Those references identify where the name appears, while the surrounding verse text is needed to explain the person’s specific role in each passage.

e.h: To Bury or Hold a Funeral
e.t: This Greek LXX verb means “bury” or “have a funeral for.” It describes the act of placing a dead person in burial and can also refer more broadly to carrying out funeral rites. The word occurs 130 times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, showing that it is a recurring term for burial rather than a rare or specialized expression. Its exact force in any passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central meaning remains the act of burying the dead.

This Greek verb means to determine or will: it describes what someone decides, desires, or is willing to do. It can express a settled choice or intention rather than merely a passing thought. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 130 times, including both the Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, so it is used broadly for human decisions and willing action. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This word means “harvest”: the gathering of crops when they are ready. It is a noun used for the produce gathered and, by extension, the season or time associated with gathering it. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears 32 times, mainly in passages concerning the yearly cycles of sowing and reaping, agricultural offerings, and the timing of events. Its use from Genesis through Sirach shows a consistent connection with the expected gathering of what has grown. The precise force in any particular verse depends on its surrounding context.

This Greek LXX noun means “hair,” referring to the strands growing on a person’s body. It is used for hair considered in ordinary descriptions and in laws that examine changes in a person’s skin and hair. The word occurs 43 times in the Greek LXX corpus, chiefly in Leviticus and Exodus, and is also found in Psalms, Samuel, Daniel, and deuterocanonical writings. Its basic sense remains literal and physical rather than symbolic.

Iasan is a proper name, referring to a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Samuel 23:32. The available wording identifies the name itself but does not provide enough surrounding verse text to explain anything further about the person or the role he has in that passage. Its meaning as a lexical entry is therefore simply the personal name Iasan.

This Greek LXX noun refers to something placatory—something connected with appeasement or the making of peace. It can describe an object or provision intended to settle offense and restore favorable relations. The word occurs 28 times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX corpus, with its use concentrated especially in Exodus, Leviticus, and Ezekiel. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

Isbakōm, also rendered Izvakom, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in 1 Chronicles 26:7. Because the name itself does not express a broader concept, its main significance is identifying a particular person in that genealogy or record. The precise role of the person named depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but the lexical meaning supplied here is simply the name Isbakōm or Izvakom.

This verb means to act basely or to plot evil. It describes deliberate wrongdoing or the planning of harmful conduct, rather than merely making a mistake. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 3 Maccabees 7:9. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense centers on acting wickedly or devising evil. The word functions as a verb, expressing what someone does or intends to do.

This Greek LXX verb means “beautiful,” describing something as beautiful or becoming beautiful. It functions as an action word rather than simply naming a person or thing. In this LXX corpus, it occurs twice, both within one verse in Song of Songs, and the available rendering is “beautiful.” The word’s precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding verse text, but its central meaning remains the expression of beauty. It is distinct here as a Greek LXX word, not a Greek New Testament entity.

This Greek LXX adjective describes someone or something as “strong; staunch.” It points to firmness, strength, or steadfastness rather than weakness or instability. The word appears six times in the Greek LXX deuterocanonical books, including 2 Maccabees, 3 Maccabees, and 4 Maccabees. Its precise emphasis in any particular sentence depends on what person, object, or quality it describes, but its central sense remains strength and dependable firmness.

This Greek LXX noun means “crying out against.” It names an act of raising a voiced protest or complaint directed against someone or something. The word focuses on the outcry itself rather than describing the person who makes it or the matter being challenged. It occurs once in the deuterocanonical LXX corpus, in Sirach 35:15. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, which is not included here.

This Greek LXX verb means to “dash down” or “break in pieces.” It describes forceful action that brings something down or causes it to be shattered. As a verb, it expresses an action rather than a person, object, or quality. The word occurs six times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Scripture represented here, including four times in Psalms and once each in Hosea and Sirach. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on what is being acted upon and the surrounding sentence.

This Greek LXX verb means “set upright”: to put something or someone into a firm, proper, or corrected position. It describes an action rather than a person or object, so its exact sense in a passage depends on what is being set upright. The word occurs 26 times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, showing repeated use for restoring or establishing something properly. It appears from 1 Kings through 2 Maccabees, including passages in Proverbs, Chronicles, Psalms, and Ezekiel.

This Greek LXX noun means “bed,” referring to a piece of furniture used for sleeping or resting. It can describe an ordinary household bed and, depending on the surrounding passage, a couch or resting place. The word occurs 40 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, from Genesis through Song of Songs. Its basic meaning remains concrete and straightforward: a place where someone lies down. The exact significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding context.

This word means “mixed wine,” referring to wine prepared by combining it with another substance or liquid. It is a noun, so it names the resulting drink rather than describing an action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Song of Songs 7:3. Because the verse text and surrounding context are not included here, the word’s precise poetic force in that passage cannot be stated beyond its basic meaning. Its central idea remains a prepared or blended wine.

This Greek LXX noun means “bean,” referring to an edible seed or legume. It appears twice in the Greek Old Testament represented here, once in 2 Samuel and once in Ezekiel. Its use is concrete and ordinary: it identifies a food item rather than an action, quality, person, or abstract idea. The word’s basic meaning is therefore straightforward—a bean used as food. Its precise role in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, which is not included here.

Lasthenes, also rendered Lasthenis, is a proper name identifying a person. It is not a general word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament collection represented here, the name occurs twice, both times in 1 Maccabees 11:31–32. The surrounding verse text would be needed to explain that person’s role in those passages; the name itself simply identifies him.

This Greek LXX verb means “ransom”: to secure someone’s release or recovery by paying a price. It describes an action rather than a person or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 98 times, making it a recurring word for deliverance through ransom, especially in passages concerning Israel, persons, or things that may be released or reclaimed. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding context.

This Greek LXX noun means a lump or cake: a compact piece or mass of something. It names a physical object rather than an action or quality. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, at Bel and the Dragon 1:27. Without the surrounding verse text, the exact object and force of the word cannot be described further. Its central sense remains a formed lump or cake.

This word means “grandmother,” referring to the mother of someone’s parent. It is a noun naming a family relationship. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 16:9. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included, the word’s basic meaning is clear, while its precise role in that sentence depends on the context. The term identifies an older female ancestor within a family, rather than expressing an action, quality, or abstract idea.

This Greek verb means to change one’s way of life. It describes a deliberate alteration in how a person lives, suggesting a change in conduct or daily manner rather than merely a change of opinion. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 4 Maccabees 8:8. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning is a changed pattern of living.

This verb means “resettle”: to move people from one place and establish them in another. It describes relocation rather than merely traveling, especially when a population is transferred to a different land or home. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs eight times, including passages in Chronicles, Jeremiah, Lamentations, Hosea, and Amos. Its exact force in any individual verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains the enforced or arranged movement of people to a new place.

This noun means “ant lion,” the name of a creature. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears only once, in Job 4:11, so its meaning is established as a specific creature name rather than a repeated description of human behavior or an action. It functions as a noun, identifying what is being mentioned. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding text, which is not included here.

This is a proper name meaning “Mōabi” or “Moavi,” a designation associated with Moab. It functions as a name rather than a word describing an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, in Ezra 9:1. Since the verse text and surrounding passage are not included, the precise reference of the name there depends on that context.

This noun means “prompting; warning”: an act of urging someone toward attention or a needed response. It describes a spoken or expressed appeal rather than a person or object. In the Greek Old Testament, this word appears once, in Wisdom 16:6. The reference identifies its location, but the word’s precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, which are not included here. Its central idea remains a timely prompt or warning intended to draw attention.

This noun means a “dwelling”—a place where someone lives or stays. It refers generally to a home, residence, or habitation rather than to a person or action. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 11:2. The surrounding verse would be needed to explain how the word functions in that particular sentence, but its basic meaning is a dwelling place.

This adjective means “at dawn,” referring to the early part of the day when daylight begins. It describes something occurring or being present in the morning’s first light, rather than later in the day. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it appears three times, including once in Job and twice in 3 Maccabees. Its exact force in any sentence depends on what person, action, or thing it describes.

This Greek LXX verb means “antiquate” or “grow old.” It describes something becoming old, worn, or belonging to an earlier stage rather than remaining new. The word is used 26 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings preserved in the LXX corpus, including passages in Leviticus, Joshua, Job, Psalms, Isaiah, and Sirach. Its precise force depends on whether the sentence speaks of a person, an object, or something passing away, but its central idea remains becoming old or outdated.

gl: wandering from reason; out of one's wits
d: wandering from reason; out of one's wits

e.t: This word describes someone who is “wandering from reason; out of one's wits”—a person whose thinking has departed from sound judgment. It functions as a noun, naming such a person rather than describing an action. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, in Wisdom 5:20. That single occurrence supports a focused meaning, while the surrounding verse would be needed to explain the word’s particular force there.

This noun means “father-in-law,” the father of someone’s spouse. It identifies a family relationship created through marriage rather than a person’s own father. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, the word occurs five times, including passages in Genesis, 1 Samuel, and 1 Maccabees.
